advisor.summary: A dependent care assistance program funded by §125 salary reduction lets an employee pay for work-enabling child or dependent care with dollars excluded from both income tax and FICA — a stack no simple deduction matches. OBBBA raised the §129 exclusion to $7,500 ($3,750 for married filing separately) beginning in 2026, the first permanent increase since the limit was set. Excluded dollars reduce the §21 credit expense base dollar-for-dollar, so run the FSA-versus-credit comparison — though above the lowest brackets the exclusion nearly always wins. Owner-sponsored plans face §129(d) testing, including the 25% shareholder-concentration limit, which stops owners from steering the benefit to themselves. The engine models the election as a W-2 wage exclusion at income-tax rates only; the FICA savings are real but sit outside the modeled burden, so the modeled number is conservative.
mechanics: The employee elects up to $7,500 (2026; $3,750 MFS) of salary reduction through a §125 cafeteria plan; the elected amount never reaches Box 1 wages and stays out of Social Security and Medicare wages under §3121(a)(18).

Qualifying care follows §21: care for a child under 13, or for a spouse or dependent incapable of self-care, incurred so the taxpayer — and a spouse, if married — can work; day camps and preschool qualify, overnight camps and K-12 tuition do not.

The exclusion is capped at the lower-earning spouse's earned income, and every excluded dollar shrinks the §21 credit expense base — the two benefits never stack on the same dollars, and Form 2441 reconciles them.
Elections lock for the plan year absent a qualifying status change, and unspent balances forfeit — set the election from documented, predictable care costs, not from the cap.

Owner-sponsored plans face §129(d) nondiscrimination testing, including the rule that no more than 25% of benefits may go to >5% owners and their spouses and dependents — a solo owner cannot concentrate the benefit on their own family.

The engine excludes the election from W-2 wages and lets the deterministic tables price the income-tax effect; the employee-side FICA savings are additional and intentionally left outside the modeled delta.

authority.note: The dependent care assistance exclusion — the annual limit, the earned-income caps, and the §129(d) nondiscrimination rules, including the 25% owner-concentration test.
Lifted the exclusion to $7,500 ($3,750 MFS) for taxable years beginning in 2026.
The cafeteria-plan salary-reduction mechanism; elections stay irrevocable for the year absent a qualifying status change.
The child and dependent care credit, whose expense base is reduced by §129 exclusions — the comparison every client needs run.
Excludes §129 benefits from FICA wages — the payroll-tax layer an ordinary deduction cannot reach.
Reports DCAP benefits and provider identification, and enforces the §21 coordination that polices double-claiming.

requirements: W-2 wages from an employer — including the client's own entity — sponsoring a §125 plan with a dependent care feature, elected before the plan year begins.
A qualifying individual — a child under 13, or a spouse or dependent incapable of self-care — plus care that lets both spouses work (student and incapacity exceptions aside).
Provider name, address, and TIN captured for Form 2441 reporting.
For owner-sponsored plans, §129(d) testing, including the 25% owner-concentration limit.
risks: The leading failure mode is administrative, not doctrinal: Form 2441 reconciles W-2 Box 10 against claimed expenses, so double-claiming the §21 credit on excluded dollars or omitting provider information surfaces at filing — there is no meaningful case law because the matching catches it first.
Over-election forfeits real dollars; the use-it-or-lose-it rule has no equitable exception.
Owner-heavy plans that fail §129(d) testing convert the owner's benefits back into taxable wages.
Care paid to the taxpayer's own child under 19, or to a claimed dependent, never qualifies.
MFS filers cap out at $3,750, and single-earner couples fail the work-enabling test unless the student or incapacity exception applies.
stateNotes: Conformity: states starting from federal AGI conform to the exclusion automatically, including the 2026 increase; a handful of states offer their own dependent-care credits worth weighing against the excluded expenses.
PTET: no PTET interaction — this is an individual payroll election, and the excluded wages never touch a pass-through entity's income base.
Missouri: conforms through the federal AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121); excluded dependent-care dollars stay off the Missouri return, with no addback.
reviewChecklist: Documented care costs support the election amount — no cap-chasing.
The §129-versus-§21 comparison is in the file, run at the client's actual marginal rate.
Provider TIN information collected; Form 2441 will reconcile cleanly.
If the plan belongs to the client's own entity, §129(d) testing — including the 25% concentration limit — is complete for the year.
Earned income confirmed for both spouses, or a student/incapacity exception documented.

client.teaser: Pay for childcare with paycheck money that skips income tax and payroll tax.
client.headline: Up to $7,500 of childcare paid with pre-tax dollars
plainEnglish: If you pay for daycare, preschool, after-school care, or summer day camp so you can work, part of it can come out of your paycheck before taxes. No income tax. No Social Security or Medicare tax either.
The limit is $7,500 a year starting in 2026 — up from $5,000 before. For many families, that puts well over two thousand dollars a year back in their pocket.

You pick your amount once a year, and money you set aside but do not spend is lost. So we set the number from your real childcare costs. We also check it against the childcare tax credit and pick whichever saves more.
client.analogy: Think of it as an express lane for your childcare money — the same bills get paid, but the tax tollbooth never sees them.
benefits: Up to $7,500 of care paid with money that is never taxed
Skips payroll tax too — something a normal deduction cannot do
Covers daycare, preschool, after-school care, and day camps
Runs through payroll, so there is nothing extra to track all year
steps: WE add up your expected care costs and compare this account to the childcare credit.
WE set the election amount so nothing goes unused.
YOU enroll at open enrollment and keep your provider's tax ID handy.
WE file the year-end form that ties it all together.
clientCommitments: Give us your care provider's name and tax ID number
Tell us if your childcare needs change during the year
Spend the account only on care that qualifies

annualMaintenance: Reset the election at each open enrollment from updated care costs
Re-run the FSA-versus-credit comparison as income and family facts change
Confirm the Form 2441 reconciliation at filing
deliverables: Election worksheet with the FSA-versus-credit comparison
